name: Trepanning

image.caption: Dr John Clarke trepanning a skull operation

lead: Trepanning is surgery that drills or scrapes a hole in the skull. It is among the oldest known surgical procedures and today survives in neurosurgery as burr holes and craniotomy. In looksmaxxing and fringe-biohacking circles, the related claim is that opening the skull boosts 'brain blood volume', lifting mood and energy and so how a person carries themselves.
The modern movement began with Dutch librarian Bart Huges, who drilled his own skull in 1965. Wikipedia reports that his claims lack research support.

paras: Modern neurosurgeons perform it under imaging and anaesthesia to treat conditions such as hematomas. Voluntary lay trepanation is not described here as a procedure.
Documented risks include infection, bleeding, brain damage and death; self-trepanation cases in the medical literature include exposed brain tissue and cerebral abscess.

chain: Claimed increase in brain blood volume
angle.text: Advocates in the Huges tradition claim it improves cerebral blood flow and mood. No human studies support a link to appearance.

lead: Trepanning, also called trepanation, trephination or burr hole, is surgery that drills or scrapes a hole into the skull. It was historically used for head injuries, intracranial pressure, epilepsy and mental disorders, and sometimes for spiritual reasons. [1]

Archaeological evidence dates it to roughly 7,000 to 10,000 years ago, with more than 1,500 trephined Neolithic skulls found worldwide. Survival rates in Andean cultures reportedly rose to about 80%. [1] Modern surgeons usually call the procedure a craniotomy, used for hematomas and neurosurgical access. [1][2]

Since the 1960s some people have had it done voluntarily for mental enhancement. Bart Huges, who wrote Homo Sapiens Correctus in 1962 and drilled his own skull in 1965, claimed it raises brain blood volume; Wikipedia states these claims lack research support. [1] Its link to looks is claimed rather than documented: advocates say it leads to a lasting euphoric state and better blood flow.

paras: Paul Broca proposed ritual purposes for trepanations on children in the 1870s, and William Osler in 1913 linked the practice to headaches, a link Wikipedia says has no credible support. [1] Chronic subdural hematoma was first successfully treated with trepanning in 1883 by Hulke. [3] Cranioplasty, repairing the hole, is described as almost as ancient as trephination, with Incan surgeons using precious metals and gourds. [4]

Huges argued trepanning was comparable to vasodilators like ginkgo biloba. Amanda Feilding and partner Joey Mellen later trepanned themselves, and Feilding's act was filmed for Heartbeat in the Brain. Claimed benefits include clairvoyance and sustained euphoria. [1] In 2000, two men in Cedar City, Utah were prosecuted for practising medicine without a license after trepanning a woman for chronic fatigue and depression. [1]

Trepanning can cause infection, bleeding, brain damage and death, with dura penetration high risk and contaminated tools raising infection risk. Self-trepanation cases in the medical literature include exposed brain tissue and a cerebral abscess. [1]
No studies found testing elective trepanation for mood, energy or appearance. Medical literature on trepanning concerns indicated uses such as subdural hematoma. [3]
